nothing about jumbo cards is published by The Pokemon Company. The two things
a reader most wants -- how big is one, and how many exist -- have NO official
answer at all, and the page says so in those words rather than picking a
number off a content farm. See `unsourced` below for the full list of what was
THE PRICES WERE READ TWICE, which is shared/graded-gate.mjs's rule applied by
hand: a research pass read every figure off PriceCharting on 21 September 2026
and a second independent pass re-read all ten the same day through
shared/pricecharting.mjs's own parser. All ten agreed to the cent. A figure
read once is not published here.

naming.note: TPCi's own retail copy says oversize -- pokemon.com product listings read "1 foil oversize card" and Pokemon Center runs an Oversize Card Sets category. The hobby says jumbo, and so does Bulbapedia, whose article is titled Jumbo cards and calls oversize the occasional alternative. Japan's official site uses ジャンボカード in product names. Both words are correct; they map to company usage and community usage, and this page uses jumbo because that is what a reader searches for.

size.standardNote: Widely agreed and not officially published by TPC anywhere we could find.
size.officialNote: The Pokemon Company publishes no dimensions for oversize cards: not on pokemon.com, not on Pokemon Center, not in the tournament rules. Official Pokemon Center Japan listings give the package size only. Everything below is somebody measuring their own cards.

measurements.note: a second hobbyist measurement, agrees on height and not on width
if right, Japanese jumbos are their own larger size. No official confirmation.

size.eras: There are at least two international sizes and the change is sourced even though the numbers are not: Bulbapedia records that jumbos got smaller starting with the Meowth VMAX jumbo in the Sword & Shield era, and TPC then shipped its first official oversize card binder, sized for the new smaller cards and first given away through a GameStop campaign the week of April 26, 2020.

boxToppers.headline: A box topper is not a jumbo, and almost every expensive one is a box topper
boxToppers.body: The marketplaces file them together, and it hides the most useful fact on this page. A modern jumbo is roughly 136 x 187 mm. A Wizards-era box topper -- the oversized card that sat on top of a booster box in Legendary Collection, Aquapolis and Skyridge -- is about 90 x 126 mm: oversized, but nowhere near jumbo size. Six of the nine most valuable cards ranked below are box toppers, and a seventh is a magazine insert. If you came here for the most valuable jumbo, it is Shadow Lugia, and both cards above it on the list are box toppers.

legality.answer: No. Jumbo cards cannot be used in sanctioned play.
legality.ruling: The Pokemon Rulings Compendium carries a ruling attributed to the TPCi Rules Team, dated August 4, 2022: a deck of uniformly sized jumbo cards is not usable in a sanctioned tournament, because only cards released for play at standard size are legal, and a jumbo is an artistic representation of the legal card.
legality.twist: The official handbook itself says nothing about size. The current Play! Pokemon TCG Tournament Handbook, revised September 1, 2026, never uses the words jumbo or oversize and specifies no card dimensions. Its legality section asks only that cards be genuine, format legal, in the right language and unmarked.
legality.story: Which is how, at the 2022 North America International Championships, a player entered a legal 60 card deck built entirely out of jumbo cards and the judges ruled it playable on the spot -- there was no size rule to break. The Compendium ruling is dated after that tournament.
legality.dateNote: Bulbapedia's footnote dates the ruling April 8, 2022 and the Compendium's own page says August 4, 2022. The Compendium's date is used here: it is the primary source and it is the one that fits, because NAIC 2022 was in late June.

howYouGetThem.dontNote: This comes from the sources, not a guess. Searching all 395 entries of Bulbapedia's international jumbo list turns up no Elite Trainer Box, tin, mini tin, blister or Build & Battle Box, and Bulbapedia's own Elite Trainer Box article lists the contents as boosters, sleeves, dividers, dice, a code card and a regular size promo. That covers the list rather than every product ever made, so read it as "do not normally" rather than "never".
howYouGetThem.europe: One quirk worth knowing: during the XY and Sun & Moon eras TPCi could not ship figures inside TCG products to Europe, so European versions of those products swapped the figure for a jumbo card. Sometimes a different jumbo than the North American release had.

history.what: The earliest jumbo we can source: a Pikachu, Jigglypuff and Clefairy insert in the July 1997 issue of CoroCoro Comic, Japan, out June 15, 1997.

The magazine and prize era. CoroCoro inserts run steadily; the first international jumbo we can source is a Base Set Pikachu in Top Deck Magazine, February 2000. Wizards of the Coast hands out Best of Game winner jumbos through BattleZone (2002-03) and e-League (2003-04).
Distribution moves decisively into sealed boxed product, starting in the Diamond & Pearl era with the Darkrai Premium Box and the Dialga and Palkia Premium Boxes.
Jumbos shrink, from the Meowth VMAX jumbo onward, and TPC ships its first official oversize card binder.

historyNote: A retailer blog dates the first jumbo to a 2000 Base Set Pikachu. That is wrong, and it is wrong in an interesting way: it misses three years of Japanese CoroCoro inserts because it is only looking at English releases.

counts.note: Nobody publishes a total -- not The Pokemon Company, not TPCi. The three biggest public counts measure different things and none is official: Bulbapedia's list of international jumbos holds 395 entries and leaves out Japanese magazine jumbos; its jumbo category holds 409 pages including Japanese ones; and TCGplayer's jumbo group holds 345 products, filed its own way. About 89% of Bulbapedia's names appear in TCGplayer's group, and neither list contains the other.

images.note: The card pictures on this page have OVERSIZE CARD stamped across them, and that is not our doing. TCGplayer watermarks its oversize scans, and it is the only site with jumbo pictures at any scale: 328 of the 345 products in its group have one, and roughly 96% of those carry the diagonal band. TCGdex, which supplies every other card picture on this site, has no jumbo pictures at all. So the choice was a stamped picture or none, and a stamped picture still shows you which card it is.

value.name: Charizard
value.why: One oversized reverse holo topper sat on top of each booster box, so supply is capped at one per box ever opened. PSA's own set registry article notes toppers are prone to edge and surface damage, which is why high grades are scarce.

value.name: Charizard
value.why: A Crystal Transparent box topper, one per booster box, out of a set with a famously small print run.

value.name: Shadow Lugia
value.why: The most valuable actual jumbo on this list. It came out alongside Pokemon XD: Gale of Darkness, and it is the only jumbo of a Shadow Pokemon. PriceCharting records no Grade 9 or PSA 10 sales for it at all.

value.name: Mewtwo
value.why: One of the four Legendary Collection toppers, same one per box supply.

value.name: Dark Blastoise
value.why: The most valuable card in TCGplayer's own jumbo group, where the Charizard toppers carry no market price at all.

value.name: Ho-oh
value.why: The second Skyridge Crystal Transparent topper.

value.name: Charizard
value.why: A magazine insert rather than a short print. This one is expensive because it is Charizard and it is old, not because it is scarce.

value.name: Mew ex
value.why: Region lock, not age. It was exclusive to the Brazilian 151 Mew ex and Mewtwo Special Collection; every other region got a different box.

valueNote: Ranked on PriceCharting's ungraded price, read {checked} and checked twice. Seven of the nine are box toppers or a magazine insert rather than modern jumbos, which is the point the section above makes.

baseline.headline: Most jumbo cards are worth a few dollars
baseline.body: A ranked list is misleading on its own, because the typical jumbo is not rare and was never meant to be. Anything that came in a collection box or a premium box from roughly 2016 onward generally sells raw for a few dollars.
baseline.averages: Two price trackers put the average across the category at $21 and $34. Those are not typical prices: they are averages, pulled up by a handful of $300 to $900 cards. Nobody publishes a median, which is why this section says "a few dollars" rather than putting a number on it.
